name: High-Bypass Turbofans
flavor: The JT9D, CF6, and RB211 entered service on the first wide-bodies in the early 1970s, moving most of a turbofan's thrust into a large, slow-spinning bypass airflow instead of the hot exhaust core. Fuel burn per seat fell sharply overnight — the single biggest efficiency leap of the jet age.

name: Winglets
flavor: NASA engineer Richard Whitcomb's upturned wingtip devices, tested through the late 1970s, cut the drag caused by wingtip vortices. What began as a modification for business jets spread to airliners over the following two decades, quietly trimming a few percent off every flight's fuel bill.

name: Digital Engine Control
flavor: Full Authority Digital Engine Control, standard by the 1990s, replaced hydromechanical fuel scheduling with software that trims each engine's burn to the exact thrust needed for the current phase of flight, rather than the wide margins a mechanical governor had to leave for safety.

name: Composite Airframes
flavor: The 787 and A350, entering service in 2011 and 2014, built most of their structure from carbon-fibre composite rather than aluminum. A lighter airframe needs less thrust to move the same payload the same distance — one of the few efficiency gains that comes from the structure itself, not the engines.

name: Geared Turbofans
flavor: Pratt & Whitney's PW1000G, flying commercially from 2016, added a reduction gearbox between the fan and the low-pressure turbine — letting each spin at its own ideal speed for the first time. A genuinely new architecture for the turbofan, not a refinement of the old one.
